explanation: Polysemantic. It fires strongly on mid-word subword pieces inside rare proper names and foreign words (Nordic words with ø/ør/j, names containing 'az' such as Ghazzawi, Pantazopoulos, Danazol, azido), and also on a scattered set of unrelated English words: 'reactive/reactively', 'risk' (in 'risk factor'), 'defensive', 'pick' (in 'at pick'), and Python dunder pieces ('/__', '.__'). Ordinary function words give only weak activation.

Fires on the verb or particle that expresses someone arriving at or joining a group or place: 'join/joined' (joined the club, joined forces), and 'to' in 'came to [place]' or 'come over to', plus 'stopped by' and 'show up'. It fires moderately on other uses of come/visit, and close to zero on unrelated tokens.

Fires on a non-initial piece of a multi-part proper name, usually right after a hyphen, '&', 'and' or a first name, where the rest of the name is predictable: Kuyavian-[P]omeranian, Davis Wright [Trem]aine, Fianna [F]áil, Clavien-[D]indo, Toys "[R]" Us, judge surnames after 'Before', and also '/apk' in the Android schemas URL. Generic subword pieces fire weakly.

Fires on 'then' used as a sequencing or contrast connective. It is strongest in 'but then' (about 80-100%), moderate for a sentence-initial 'Then' or 'and then' (about 25-65%), and only weak or occasional on other tokens.

Fires in source code, mostly JavaScript/jQuery, on the punctuation that separates a key or variable name from its value: ':' after an object key (data:, scrollTop:), ' =' in var/const declarations, and nearby argument separators like ',' and '('. It is strongest inside $.ajax-style object literals. Code tokens of other kinds fire moderately to weakly, and prose barely at all.

Fires on tokens inside Spanish or Portuguese text, especially function words such as 'de', 'la', 'a', 'y', 'para' and the opening subword pieces of Spanish/Portuguese words and place names (atendidos, Córdoba, Torcuato). It also fires weaker on other non-English or foreign-name fragments. English text does not activate it.

Fires on a semicolon that joins two clauses in prose, e.g. '...lymphomas; however', '...community; it's'. It also fires on ';' in license text and 'text/html; charset', and somewhat on relative-clause starters like 'that' or 'who' right after a noun phrase. Other clause-internal tokens fire only weakly.

Fires on runs of multiple spaces or tabs used for column alignment, e.g. padding between a field name and its type or '=' in Go structs and aligned assignments, in SQL column definitions, in docblock tags, and in ASCII tables or legal captions. It is strongest in aligned code declarations and weaker in tables and plain text.

Fires on a head noun naming something a person or device has, usually right after a possessive or article: 'account' (you already have an account, your account), 'name', 'voice', 'eyes', 'gaze', 'stories', and 'beam' in 'electron/laser beam'. Other abstract nouns ('chance', 'discussion', 'championship') fire moderately to weakly.

Fires on a single digit token inside a long digit string, such as IDs, citation numbers, patent or case numbers, page ranges, prices and years (e.g. the '9' in '1966', digits in 'pone.0204559'). It is strongest mid-number. It does not fire on the start of a short standalone number or on non-numeric text.

Fires on tokens about tech platforms and developer ecosystems ('Developers' in Google Apps Developers, android-developers, '.NET', Google+, 'schemas.android', App Store), and on words about online communities or connecting with peers ('community', 'connect with', 'a' in 'finding a health professional'). It is moderate on general software terms and weak elsewhere.
